abstract: Proteins can misfold into soluble, near-native states that act as long-lived kinetic traps with aggregation independent biological consequences. A key step toward obtaining high-resolution structures of these states is the ability to isolate/purify them. Here, we show this is possible for the Escherichia coli protein pyruvate kinase (pykF) following refolding from chemical denaturant. After controlling for aggregates the refolded (treatment) ensemble exhibits a decrease in average specific activity relative to the untreated (natively folded) sample. Size exclusion chromatography reveals two distinct populations in this treatment group, whereas the untreated group exhibits a single population. Native PAGE analysis finds that both populations from the treatment group have the same mass and electrophoretic mobility as the untreated protein, consistent with native-like global properties and oligomerization state. Functional analysis using Michaelis-Menten kinetics shows that one population retains activity comparable to the untreated sample, while the other has no detectable activity, indicating that approximately 31 +/- 17.9% (95% Confidence Interval) of refolded molecules are soluble, near-native, but non-functional. ANS fluorescence measurements probing hydrophobic surface exposure further show that the non-functional population has altered surface properties relative to the active population. Differences in these properties persist for at least four hours following renaturation, indicating the system remains out-of-equilibrium. Together, these results demonstrate that size exclusion chromatography can be used to isolate soluble, non-aggregating, misfolded states that are structurally similar to the native state yet functionally inactive. This approach provides a basis for enriching such misfolded states for subsequent high-resolution structural characterization.
